query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Liquid‐metal dealloying of a directionally segregated WTaVTi refractory high-entropy alloy in molten Cu creates a bicontinuous composite structure with a spontaneously formed, W-rich passivating interlayer that enhances high-temperature thermal conductivity and reduces helium-induced swelling compared to conventional pure W or traditional W–Cu composites.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, nominally equiatomic WTaVTi refractory high-entropy alloy with a segregated dendrite–interdendrite structure: W/Ta-rich dendrites and Ti/V-rich interdendritic channels.
generation.intervention: Immerse the WTaVTi precursor in molten Cu at 1200 °C for 96 hours (liquid-metal dealloying) to selectively extract Ti from the interdendritic regions.
generation.conditions: Processing in a vacuum-sealed silica environment at 1200 °C for 96 hours, followed by characterization from room temperature up to ~800 °C for thermal conductivity, and 25 keV He+ irradiation to assess swelling behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: A bicontinuous, directionally aligned structure comprising approximately 64 vol.% BCC RHEA ligaments interwoven with 36 vol.% nearly pure FCC Cu channels, with an approximately 300 nm thick spontaneous W-rich interlayer at each RHEA/Cu interface and minor HCP Ti-rich precipitates.
generation.mechanism: The negative heat of mixing between Ti and Cu drives the preferential dissolution of Ti from the interdendritic channels, leaving behind a framework of W, Ta, and V that forms the RHEA ligaments. The strong positive heat of mixing between W and Cu traps W at the interfaces as a passivating layer, stabilizing the bicontinuous architecture. The aligned Cu channels provide enhanced heat conduction while the complex RHEA lattice resists helium-induced defect migration, curtailing swelling.
generation.predicted_outcome: The composite is expected to achieve substantially higher thermal conductivity at high temperatures (notably above 650 °C and peaking above 1000 °C) compared to the unprocessed WTaVTi precursor and even pure W, while also exhibiting reduced helium-induced swelling and delayed blistering relative to pure W.
generation.baseline: Unprocessed WTaVTi alloy, pure W, pure Cu, and conventional W–Cu composite fabrication methods, with pure W serving as the primary irradiation baseline for helium-induced swelling studies.
generation.boundary: The expected improvements are confined to composites produced from directionally segregated WTaVTi precursors processed under the 1200 °C/96 h liquid-metal dealloying condition. Benefits are most pronounced at high service temperatures (above ~650 °C) and under low-energy He+ irradiation; extrapolation to neutron irradiation or other high-energy environments remains untested.
generation.uncertainty: Although microstructural mechanisms support the predicted enhancement in thermal transport and irradiation resistance, quantitative performance improvements may vary due to processing consistency and the limited scope of irradiation testing. Extrapolated benefits above 1000 °C and under different irradiation conditions remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the WTaVTi precursor processed with and without the liquid-metal dealloying step. Confirm the formation of the bicontinuous structure and W-rich interlayers using SEM, TEM-EDS, and XRD. Measure temperature-dependent thermal conductivity using laser-flash analysis from room temperature to 800 °C and perform 25 keV He+ implantation followed by AFM analysis to quantify swelling and blister onset. Compare mechanical properties with nanoindentation tests on Cu channels against those of pure Cu.
measurements: SEM/TEM-EDS imaging and XRD phase analysis
AFM measurements of swelling height and blister/cracking onset after He+ irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the processed composite does not demonstrate a significant increase in thermal conductivity at high temperatures compared to both the unprocessed WTaVTi and pure W baselines, or if its He+-induced swelling is not measurably lower than that of pure W.
